analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers $50 per ton of carbon and pays every taxpayer a $1,000 refundable credit.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first committee and died at the end of the 117th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a fee of $50 on every ton of carbon contained in coal, oil, and gas produced in or imported into the United States, rising each year with inflation. That fee would be paid by coal mines and oil and gas wells, who would likely pass much of it on in fuel prices. The bill returns the money to households: every taxpayer, and each dependent, would get a $1,000 refundable credit — cash paid even to people who owe no income tax — phased out only above roughly $157,000 of income for a single filer. A family of four would receive $4,000 a year. The idea is that the rebate would exceed most households' higher energy costs, so most people would come out ahead financially while the higher price of fossil fuels pushes the economy toward cleaner energy.
analysis.who_benefits: Households earning under about $157,000 (single) or $314,000 (joint) receive a refundable $1,000 credit for each taxpayer and dependent — money paid even if they owe no tax. Because a $50-per-ton carbon fee raises prices mainly in proportion to how much fuel a household burns, most lower- and middle-income households would receive more in rebates than they pay in higher fuel prices. People who reduce their fuel use keep more of the rebate. The policy also addresses climate change, whose costs fall on everyone.

how_it_helps.text: Gives every individual taxpayer a $1,000 refundable credit, plus $1,000 for each dependent, paid even to households that owe no income tax.
Phases the credit out only above $157,000 of income for single filers and $314,000 for joint filers, so it goes to the large majority of households.
Prices the carbon in coal, oil, and gas at $50 per ton, rising annually with inflation, which is designed to make cleaner energy relatively cheaper over time.
Applies the fee to imported fuel as well as domestic production, so domestic producers are not put at a disadvantage against imports.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mines and oil and gas producers pay the $50-per-ton fee on their output. They can be expected to pass a large share of it through to consumers in higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, electricity, and goods made with fossil energy. Households above the phaseout thresholds get little or no credit to offset those higher prices. Energy-intensive industries that cannot quickly switch to cleaner inputs also bear higher costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The carbon fee would raise gasoline, heating, and electricity prices, and producers would pass a large share of the $50-per-ton fee through to consumers; households above the income phaseout get no rebate to offset it.

A family that received the credit could still be worse off if its energy costs — or prices for goods shipped and manufactured with fossil energy — rose by more than $1,000 per person, a real risk in regions and occupations that depend heavily on fuel and driving.
The bill specifies no dedicated funding for workers or communities dependent on coal, oil, and gas jobs, which would face pressure as production becomes more expensive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design follows the standard carbon-dividend model: the rebate is refundable, universal up to high incomes, and per person, so most households — especially lower-income ones — would likely receive more than they pay in higher fuel prices. That makes the net financial effect favorable for most working people, while the price signal does the long-term work of cutting emissions. The honest costs are the price increases borne by households above the phaseout, by high-fuel-use households whose rebate may not cover the pass-through, and by fossil-fuel-dependent regions that get no targeted transition help in this bill. The bill's fatal weakness was political: it attracted no cosponsors, which in practice means no constituency for the trade-offs it asks energy-producing states to accept.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee when introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Sean Patrick Maloney introduced the bill on July 28, 2022, in the final months of the 117th Congress.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles tax legislation, and no further action was taken on it.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in the House.

The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the bill ever reaching the House floor; bills that are not passed by both chambers before a Congress ends die and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and gas producers are better off because the bill died: no $50-per-ton carbon fee was ever imposed on their output, and no nationwide carbon pricing took effect. Households also never saw the offsetting $1,000-per-person rebate, which died with it.

for.name: Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee; recruited no cosponsors before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the remainder of the 117th Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split on the merits is recorded — only that no member of either party signed on.

industries.industry: Coal mining and oil and gas producers
industries.note: The bill imposes a $50-per-ton fee on the carbon in their output, including imports, rising with inflation each year. The industry's interest in avoiding the fee runs against the policy's purpose of pricing carbon emissions, though consumers would share the cost through higher fuel prices.

industries.industry: Energy consumers, including utilities and fuel-heavy industries
industries.note: They would pay higher prices as the fee passes through, but households below the phaseout thresholds receive a $1,000-per-person rebate that likely exceeds typical household energy cost increases; heavy industrial fuel users get no rebate and would face higher costs.
